contentBlocks.text: Last week you described motion mathematically. This week: forces, the actual cause of motion changes!

Newton's First Law states that an object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at a constant velocity, unless acted on by a net (unbalanced) force — this tendency to resist a change in motion is called inertia. This connects directly to last week's velocity and acceleration content: without a net force, there's simply no acceleration, so velocity never changes. Explain why passengers in a car feel pushed backward when the car suddenly accelerates forward, using Newton's First Law.
You just learned Newton's First Law and inertia! Tomorrow we'll learn the Second Law, connecting force directly to acceleration.

objectives: State Newton's First Law and define inertia

differentiationTips: Struggling: use a simple, familiar example — a ball resting on a table stays put until someone pushes it, and once rolling, it would keep rolling forever on a frictionless surface
Ready for more: ask the child why a car passenger wearing a seatbelt feels a smaller version of this same push during sudden braking, not just sudden acceleration

teacherGuide.answerKey: The passengers' bodies have inertia and tend to stay at their original velocity (at rest, before the car accelerated) — as the car and seat push the passengers' bodies forward with them, the passengers feel this as a backward push relative to the accelerating car, even though it's really their own inertia resisting the change in motion.
